topic: Fair Housing, Human Rights Law & Anti-Discrimination
question: The federal Fair Housing Act was originally enacted in 1968 as Title VIII of the Civil Rights Act of 1968. Which protected classes did the original 1968 law cover, before later amendments expanded the list?
choice_a: Race, color, religion, and national origin only
choice_b: Race, color, religion, national origin, sex, and disability
choice_c: All seven of today's federal protected classes, unchanged since 1968
choice_d: Only race and religion
explanation: The original 1968 Fair Housing Act (Title VIII of the Civil Rights Act of 1968) protected only race, color, religion, and national origin. Sex was added in 1974, and disability and familial status were added by the Fair Housing Amendments Act of 1988, bringing the federal total to today's seven classes.
source_note: 42 U.S.C. Section 3601 et seq. (Fair Housing Act, original 1968 enactment history)

topic: Fair Housing, Human Rights Law & Anti-Discrimination
question: In what year was 'sex' added as a protected class under the federal Fair Housing Act, prior to the 1988 additions of disability and familial status?
explanation: Congress amended the Fair Housing Act in 1974 to add sex as a protected class -- six years after the original 1968 Act and fourteen years before the 1988 Fair Housing Amendments Act added disability and familial status.
source_note: 42 U.S.C. Section 3601 et seq. (1974 amendment adding sex as a protected class)

topic: Fair Housing, Human Rights Law & Anti-Discrimination
question: The Fair Housing Amendments Act of 1988 expanded the federal Fair Housing Act's protected classes from four to seven. Which two classes did the 1988 amendments add?
choice_a: Disability and familial status
choice_b: Sex and national origin
choice_c: Lawful source of income and sexual orientation
choice_d: Age and marital status
explanation: The Fair Housing Amendments Act of 1988 added disability and familial status as federally protected classes, and also introduced the concepts of reasonable accommodation and reasonable modification for persons with disabilities.
source_note: Fair Housing Amendments Act of 1988 (Pub. L. 100-430)

topic: Fair Housing, Human Rights Law & Anti-Discrimination
question: A landlord refuses to rent an apartment to an 82-year-old applicant, telling her he 'prefers younger tenants who will be around longer.' Under New York law, what has the landlord likely violated?
choice_a: Executive Law Section 296(5), since age is a protected class under New York's Human Rights Law even though age is not one of the federal Fair Housing Act's seven protected classes
choice_b: Nothing, since age discrimination in housing is not prohibited anywhere in the United States
choice_c: Only a federal violation, since age is one of the federal Fair Housing Act's seven classes
choice_d: Nothing, since landlords may set any age preference they wish for tenants
explanation: Age is a protected class under New York's Human Rights Law (Executive Law Section 296(5)) even though it is not among the federal Fair Housing Act's seven protected classes -- illustrating that New York licensees must comply with the state's broader list, not just the federal floor.
source_note: Executive Law Section 296(5) (age as a NY-specific protected class, beyond the federal seven)

topic: Fair Housing, Human Rights Law & Anti-Discrimination
question: An unmarried couple applies to rent an apartment together, and the landlord refuses, stating a policy of renting only to married couples or single individuals. Under New York law, what protected class does this implicate?
choice_a: Marital status, which is protected under New York's Human Rights Law though not among the federal Fair Housing Act's seven classes
choice_b: Familial status, since the couple has no children
choice_c: No protected class is implicated, since marital-status preferences are lawful everywhere
choice_d: National origin
explanation: Marital status is a protected class under New York's Human Rights Law (Executive Law Section 296(5)), meaning a landlord may not refuse to rent based on whether applicants are married -- a protection that goes beyond the federal Fair Housing Act's seven classes, which do not include marital status.
source_note: Executive Law Section 296(5) (marital status as a NY-specific protected class)

topic: Fair Housing, Human Rights Law & Anti-Discrimination
question: A landlord declines to rent to an active-duty National Guard member, explaining that deployment risk makes the tenancy 'too unpredictable.' Which New York protected class is implicated, one that is not among the federal Fair Housing Act's seven classes?
choice_a: Military status
choice_b: Familial status
choice_c: National origin
choice_d: Disability
explanation: Military status is a protected class under New York's Human Rights Law (Executive Law Section 296(5)). Refusing housing to a tenant because of their military service or deployment status is unlawful discrimination in New York, even though military status is not one of the federal Fair Housing Act's seven protected classes.
source_note: Executive Law Section 296(5) (military status as a NY-specific protected class)

topic: Fair Housing, Human Rights Law & Anti-Discrimination
question: Under the federal Fair Housing Act's familial status protections, which of the following individuals is included within the protected class?
choice_a: A pregnant woman, and any person in the process of securing legal custody of a child under 18
choice_b: Only married couples with biological children already living with them
choice_c: Only households with two or more children
choice_d: Only households where a child is already over the age of 18
explanation: Familial status protection under the Fair Housing Act extends to pregnant women and to any person in the process of securing legal custody of a child under 18 (such as through adoption or a pending custody proceeding), not just households where children are already present.
source_note: 42 U.S.C. Section 3602(k) (Fair Housing Act -- definition of familial status)

topic: Fair Housing, Human Rights Law & Anti-Discrimination
question: A tenant with a documented disability requests permission to keep an emotional support animal despite the building's no-pets policy. May the landlord charge the standard pet deposit and monthly pet fee for the animal?
choice_a: No -- an assistance animal is not a pet under fair housing law, and pet fees, deposits, or added rent may not be charged for it, though the tenant remains liable for any actual damage the animal causes
choice_b: Yes, the same pet fees apply regardless of the animal's assistance function
choice_c: Yes, but only if the animal lacks formal training or certification
choice_d: No fee may be charged, but the landlord may require proof the animal is professionally certified before allowing it
explanation: Under the Fair Housing Act, an assistance animal (including an emotional support animal) is not treated as a pet -- housing providers cannot charge pet fees, deposits, or additional rent for it, and cannot require certification or formal training as a condition of allowing it. The tenant does remain financially responsible for any actual damage the animal causes.
source_note: 42 U.S.C. Section 3604(f) (Fair Housing Act -- assistance animals, no pet fee rule, no certification requirement)

topic: Fair Housing, Human Rights Law & Anti-Discrimination
question: Under New York's Human Rights Law, is it separately unlawful to retaliate against a tenant who filed a housing discrimination complaint or requested a reasonable accommodation?
choice_a: Yes -- Executive Law Section 296(7) independently prohibits retaliation against anyone who opposed a discriminatory practice, filed a complaint, testified, or requested a reasonable accommodation
choice_b: No, retaliation is only prohibited in the employment context, not in housing
choice_c: No, a landlord may take any adverse action against a tenant who files a discrimination complaint
choice_d: Retaliation is prohibited only if the underlying discrimination complaint is proven to have merit
explanation: Executive Law Section 296(7) makes retaliation an independently unlawful discriminatory practice, protecting anyone who opposed a forbidden practice, filed a complaint, testified or assisted in a proceeding, or requested a reasonable accommodation -- this protection applies regardless of whether the underlying complaint is ultimately substantiated.
source_note: Executive Law Section 296(7) (NY Human Rights Law -- retaliation protection)

topic: Fair Housing, Human Rights Law & Anti-Discrimination
question: Under New York's Human Rights Law, can a person who did not personally refuse housing, but who helped, encouraged, or pressured another party into committing a discriminatory act, also be held liable?
choice_a: Yes -- Executive Law Section 296(6) makes it unlawful to aid, abet, incite, compel, or coerce a discriminatory act, or to attempt to do so
choice_b: No, only the party who directly refused housing can ever be held liable
choice_c: No, aiding and abetting liability applies only in criminal law, never in housing discrimination cases
choice_d: Only licensed real estate brokers can be held liable for aiding or abetting discrimination
explanation: Executive Law Section 296(6) extends liability beyond the party who directly discriminates, making it unlawful for any person to aid, abet, incite, compel, or coerce a discriminatory act, or to attempt to do so -- this can reach, for example, an agent who knowingly helps a client carry out a discriminatory refusal.
source_note: Executive Law Section 296(6) (NY Human Rights Law -- aiding and abetting liability)

topic: Fair Housing, Human Rights Law & Anti-Discrimination
question: The New York City Human Rights Law protects certain classes in housing that are not separately enumerated under New York State's Human Rights Law. Which of the following is a class protected under NYC's law specifically?
choice_a: Lawful occupation and partnership status
choice_b: Race
choice_c: Disability
choice_d: Familial status
explanation: The New York City Human Rights Law protects a still-broader list than state law, including classes such as lawful occupation and partnership status that are not separately enumerated as protected classes under the state Human Rights Law -- reinforcing that NYC licensees must be aware of an additional, city-specific layer of protection.
source_note: NYC Administrative Code Section 8-107 (NYC Human Rights Law -- housing protected classes)

topic: Fair Housing, Human Rights Law & Anti-Discrimination
question: New York City's Fair Chance for Housing Act (Local Law 24 of 2024) primarily restricts a housing provider's ability to do what?
choice_a: Consider an applicant's criminal history -- limiting review to certain recent convictions and registered sex offenses, and requiring an individualized assessment and a required notice before a background check is run
choice_b: Charge a security deposit greater than one month's rent
choice_c: Require proof of income from a rental applicant
choice_d: Advertise a rental listing on a public website
explanation: The NYC Fair Chance for Housing Act restricts criminal background screening in housing, limiting reviewable history mainly to recent misdemeanor and felony convictions and registered sex offenses, excluding sealed/expunged/vacated records, and requiring housing providers to give applicants notice and an individualized assessment before denying housing based on criminal history.
source_note: NYC Local Law 24 of 2024 (Fair Chance for Housing Act, effective January 1, 2025)

topic: Fair Housing, Human Rights Law & Anti-Discrimination
question: A prospective tenant in New York City wants to file a housing discrimination complaint. May she file the same claim, based on the same facts, with both the NYC Commission on Human Rights and the NYS Division of Human Rights at the same time?
choice_a: No -- filing the same claim with one agency generally precludes also filing it with the other; a complainant must choose one administrative forum (or court) for a given claim
choice_b: Yes, filing with both agencies simultaneously is required by law
choice_c: Yes, and each agency must independently investigate and issue its own separate ruling on the identical facts
choice_d: It depends solely on which protected class is at issue
explanation: A complainant generally cannot pursue the same housing discrimination claim, based on the same facts, simultaneously with both the NYC Commission on Human Rights and the NYS Division of Human Rights (or in court) -- filing with one forum generally precludes filing the identical claim with another, so licensees should understand that complainants must elect a single forum.
source_note: hedge: general election-of-remedies principle across NYC Commission on Human Rights and NYS Division of Human Rights, well-corroborated by legal-industry sources

topic: Fair Housing, Human Rights Law & Anti-Discrimination
question: As of a 2023 amendment signed by Governor Hochul (effective February 15, 2024), how long does a complainant generally have to file a housing discrimination complaint with the NYS Division of Human Rights?
choice_a: Three years from the discriminatory act, extended from the previous one-year deadline
choice_b: Thirty days from the discriminatory act
choice_c: Ten years from the discriminatory act
choice_d: There is no deadline at all to file with the Division of Human Rights
explanation: Effective February 15, 2024, New York extended the statute of limitations for filing most Human Rights Law discrimination complaints -- including housing -- with the Division of Human Rights from one year to three years; acts that occurred before that effective date generally remain subject to the prior one-year deadline.
source_note: S.3255 (2023), amending Executive Law Section 297(5); effective February 15, 2024

topic: Fair Housing, Human Rights Law & Anti-Discrimination
question: Under the federal Fair Housing Act, what is the deadline for filing a housing discrimination complaint directly with HUD, as opposed to filing a lawsuit in federal or state court?
choice_a: One year from the occurrence (or termination) of the discriminatory practice to file with HUD; up to two years to instead file suit in court
choice_b: Ninety days to file with HUD, and no option to go to court
choice_c: There is no deadline to file with HUD, but a court suit must be filed within thirty days
choice_d: Five years to file with HUD, and no separate court option exists
explanation: Under the federal Fair Housing Act, a HUD administrative complaint must generally be filed within one year of the discriminatory act, while a private lawsuit may be filed in federal or state court within two years -- giving an aggrieved person two different avenues with two different filing deadlines.
source_note: 42 U.S.C. Section 3610 (HUD administrative complaint deadline); 42 U.S.C. Section 3613 (private civil action deadline)

topic: Fair Housing, Human Rights Law & Anti-Discrimination
question: What is the legal difference between 'disparate treatment' and 'disparate impact' as theories of housing discrimination liability?
choice_a: Disparate treatment is intentional, differential treatment of a person because of a protected characteristic; disparate impact involves a facially neutral policy that has a disproportionately adverse effect on a protected class, regardless of intent
choice_b: The two terms describe the same legal theory and are used interchangeably
choice_c: Disparate impact requires proof of intentional bias, while disparate treatment does not
choice_d: Disparate treatment applies only to lending; disparate impact applies only to advertising
explanation: Disparate treatment liability requires proof that a person was intentionally treated differently because of a protected characteristic, while disparate impact liability can arise from a facially neutral policy or practice that disproportionately harms a protected class, even without any discriminatory intent -- both are recognized theories of liability under fair housing law.
source_note: hedge: standard, well-corroborated fair housing legal doctrine (disparate treatment vs. disparate impact); Texas Dep't of Housing v. Inclusive Communities Project (2015)

topic: Fair Housing, Human Rights Law & Anti-Discrimination
question: The federal Housing for Older Persons Act (HOPA) exemption for '55 or older' housing communities generally requires which of the following?
choice_a: At least 80% of occupied units must have at least one resident age 55 or older, and the community must publish and adhere to policies demonstrating its intent to operate as 55-or-older housing
choice_b: Every single resident in the community must be at least 55 years old, with no exceptions
choice_c: The community need only advertise itself as '55 or older' with no occupancy or policy requirements
choice_d: At least 25% of units must have a resident age 55 or older
explanation: To qualify for the federal Housing for Older Persons Act's '55 or older' familial-status exemption, at least 80% of occupied units must have at least one resident aged 55 or older, and the community must publish and adhere to policies and procedures demonstrating its intent to operate as housing for older persons, including age-verification procedures.
source_note: Housing for Older Persons Act of 1995; 42 U.S.C. Section 3607(b); 24 C.F.R. Section 100.304

topic: Fair Housing, Human Rights Law & Anti-Discrimination
question: How does the federal '62 or older' housing exemption under HOPA differ from the '55 or older' exemption?
choice_a: The '62 or older' exemption applies to housing intended for, and solely occupied by, persons 62 or older, with no 80%-occupancy threshold or additional facilities/services requirement -- age alone qualifies the community
choice_b: The '62 or older' exemption requires the same 80% occupancy threshold and published policies as the '55 or older' exemption
choice_c: There is no '62 or older' exemption under federal law -- only the '55 or older' exemption exists
choice_d: The '62 or older' exemption applies only to rental housing, never to housing offered for sale
explanation: The '62 or older' HOPA exemption applies to housing intended for and solely occupied by persons 62 or older -- a simpler standard than the '55 or older' exemption, which instead requires an 80% occupancy threshold and published policies demonstrating intent to operate as older-persons housing.
source_note: Housing for Older Persons Act of 1995; 42 U.S.C. Section 3607(b)(2)(C)

topic: Fair Housing, Human Rights Law & Anti-Discrimination
question: Under the federal Fair Housing Act's religious organization exemption, a nonprofit religious organization may limit the sale or rental of dwellings it owns and operates for noncommercial purposes to persons of the same religion, EXCEPT in what circumstance?
choice_a: Where membership in the religious organization is itself restricted on account of race, color, or national origin
choice_b: The exemption has no exceptions whatsoever
choice_c: Where the dwelling is located outside of New York State
choice_d: Where the religious organization has more than 100 members
explanation: The federal Fair Housing Act's religious organization exemption allows a nonprofit religious group to prefer members of its own religion for noncommercial dwellings it owns and operates -- but the exemption is unavailable if membership in that religious organization is itself restricted based on race, color, or national origin.
source_note: 42 U.S.C. Section 3607(a) (Fair Housing Act -- religious organization exemption)

topic: Fair Housing, Human Rights Law & Anti-Discrimination
question: Under the federal Fair Housing Act's private club exemption, a private club may limit lodging it provides to its own members if which conditions are met?
choice_a: The club is not in fact open to the public, and providing the lodging is incidental to the club's primary purpose rather than a commercial operation
choice_b: Any organization calling itself a 'club,' regardless of public access, automatically qualifies
choice_c: The exemption applies only if the club charges no membership dues
choice_d: The exemption applies to any lodging the club provides, even if lodging is the club's primary commercial business
explanation: The Fair Housing Act's private club exemption is narrow: it applies only where the club is genuinely not open to the public and the lodging it provides is incidental to its primary (non-lodging) purpose, rather than being operated as a commercial lodging business.
source_note: 42 U.S.C. Section 3607 (Fair Housing Act -- private club exemption)

topic: Fair Housing, Human Rights Law & Anti-Discrimination
question: The federal 'for sale by owner' exemption under 42 U.S.C. Section 3603(b)(1) is distinct from the 'Mrs. Murphy' owner-occupied building exemption. What does the 'for sale by owner' exemption cover?
choice_a: A private individual owner who does not own more than three single-family homes at a time, sells or rents without the use of a real estate broker or discriminatory advertising, and is limited to no more than one such sale in any 24-month period without owning the home
choice_b: Any real estate broker who lists a for-sale-by-owner property
choice_c: Only new-construction homes sold directly by a builder
choice_d: Any property listed on the MLS regardless of who owns it
explanation: The federal Fair Housing Act's 'for sale by owner' exemption (distinct from the owner-occupied 'Mrs. Murphy' exemption) applies narrowly to a private individual who owns no more than three single-family homes at a time and sells or rents without a broker and without discriminatory advertising -- it does not apply to a licensed real estate broker or salesperson acting in that capacity.
source_note: 42 U.S.C. Section 3603(b)(1) (Fair Housing Act -- 'for sale by owner' exemption)

topic: Fair Housing, Human Rights Law & Anti-Discrimination
question: How does New York's owner-occupied housing exemption under Executive Law Section 296(5) compare to the federal 'Mrs. Murphy' exemption in terms of building size?
choice_a: New York's exemption is narrower, generally applying only to owner-occupied buildings with no more than two units, compared to the federal exemption's coverage of owner-occupied buildings with up to four units
choice_b: New York's exemption is broader, covering owner-occupied buildings of any size
choice_c: The two exemptions are identical in every respect
choice_d: New York has no owner-occupied exemption of any kind
explanation: New York's Human Rights Law owner-occupied exemption is narrower than its federal counterpart -- generally limited to buildings with no more than two units where the owner resides in one -- while the federal 'Mrs. Murphy' exemption can extend to owner-occupied buildings with up to four units, meaning a transaction exempt federally may still be covered under New York law.
source_note: Executive Law Section 296(5) (NY owner-occupied exemption, narrower than federal 'Mrs. Murphy' exemption)

topic: Fair Housing, Human Rights Law & Anti-Discrimination
question: Under the Fair Housing Act's design and construction requirements, covered multifamily dwellings of four or more units built for first occupancy after a specific date must include certain accessibility features. What is that date?
choice_a: March 13, 1991
choice_b: January 1, 1968
choice_c: July 1, 1988
choice_d: January 1, 2010
explanation: Covered multifamily dwellings (buildings with four or more units) designed and constructed for first occupancy after March 13, 1991 must include specified accessibility features, such as accessible common-use areas, usable doors, and accessible routes -- a requirement distinct from the reasonable-accommodation and reasonable-modification duties that apply to existing housing.
source_note: 42 U.S.C. Section 3604(f)(3)(C) (Fair Housing Act -- design and construction accessibility requirements)

topic: Fair Housing, Human Rights Law & Anti-Discrimination
question: Executive Law Section 296-a is a separate New York anti-discrimination statute from Section 296(5). What does Section 296-a specifically prohibit?
choice_a: Discrimination in the granting, terms, or conditions of credit -- including mortgage lending -- based on protected characteristics such as race, creed, color, national origin, sex, marital status, disability, and familial status
choice_b: Discriminatory advertising in real estate listings only
choice_c: Blockbusting specifically, and nothing else
choice_d: Discrimination in commercial leasing only, not residential
explanation: Executive Law Section 296-a addresses discrimination in credit transactions -- including mortgage lending decisions, terms, and rates -- based on protected characteristics, and (like Section 296(5)) recognizes a disparate impact theory of liability. It is a distinct statutory provision from Section 296(5)'s housing sale/rental discrimination prohibitions, reflecting that fair lending and fair housing are related but separately regulated areas.
source_note: Executive Law Section 296-a (NY Human Rights Law -- credit discrimination); NYS Department of Financial Services industry guidance

topic: Fair Housing, Human Rights Law & Anti-Discrimination
question: New York recently enacted Real Property Law Section 327-a addressing discriminatory restrictive covenants found in older recorded deeds and governing documents. What does this law generally require?
choice_a: Sellers must submit a 'restrictive covenant modification document' to strike unenforceable discriminatory language from the record, and co-ops, condos, and homeowners' associations must remove or amend such language from their governing documents
choice_b: It makes discriminatory restrictive covenants enforceable again if both parties agree
choice_c: It requires no action at all, since old restrictive covenants have always been automatically deleted from public records
choice_d: It applies only to commercial property, never to residential deeds or co-op/condo documents
explanation: Real Property Law Section 327-a requires sellers to submit a restrictive covenant modification document to formally strike unenforceable discriminatory language (based on race, religion, or national origin, for example) from recorded documents, and requires condominiums, cooperative corporations, and homeowners' associations to remove or amend such discriminatory language from their governing documents.
source_note: Real Property Law Section 327-a (recently enacted; addresses discriminatory restrictive covenants in recorded documents)

topic: Fair Housing, Human Rights Law & Anti-Discrimination
question: Under the federal Fair Housing Act, the definition of a covered 'disability' (historically termed 'handicap' in the statute) includes which three categories of individuals?
choice_a: A person with a physical or mental impairment that substantially limits one or more major life activities; a person with a record of such an impairment; and a person regarded as having such an impairment
choice_b: Only individuals currently using a wheelchair
choice_c: Only individuals who have applied for Social Security Disability benefits
choice_d: Only individuals with a permanent, as opposed to temporary, impairment
explanation: The Fair Housing Act's disability definition covers three categories: a person with an actual physical or mental impairment substantially limiting a major life activity, a person with a record of such an impairment, and a person regarded by others as having such an impairment -- even if no actual impairment exists in the third category.
source_note: 42 U.S.C. Section 3602(h) (Fair Housing Act -- definition of disability/handicap)

topic: Fair Housing, Human Rights Law & Anti-Discrimination
question: Under the federal Fair Housing Act, which individual is specifically EXCLUDED from the statutory definition of 'disability,' solely by virtue of that status?
choice_a: A current, illegal user of a controlled substance
choice_b: A person with a mobility impairment who uses a wheelchair
choice_c: A person recovering from alcoholism
choice_d: A person with a hearing impairment
explanation: The Fair Housing Act's definition of disability specifically excludes current illegal users of controlled substances (as well as individuals convicted of illegal manufacture or distribution of a controlled substance, by virtue of that status). By contrast, individuals recovering from alcoholism or past drug addiction are not excluded and remain protected.
source_note: 42 U.S.C. Section 3602(h) (Fair Housing Act -- exclusions from the definition of disability)

topic: Fair Housing, Human Rights Law & Anti-Discrimination
question: Under Real Property Law Section 441-c, what effect does an outside finding by a court or agency that a licensee engaged in unlawful housing discrimination have on a DOS license discipline proceeding?
choice_a: It constitutes presumptive evidence of untrustworthiness, subjecting the licensee to DOS discipline, potentially including license revocation
choice_b: It has no bearing whatsoever on any DOS licensing matter
choice_c: It automatically results in criminal prosecution of the licensee, with no possibility of DOS-level discipline
choice_d: DOS must independently re-litigate every underlying fact before it may even consider the outside finding
explanation: Under Real Property Law Section 441-c, a finding by any federal, state, or local agency or court of competent jurisdiction that a real estate broker or salesperson engaged in unlawful discriminatory practice while performing licensed real estate activities is presumptive evidence of untrustworthiness, subjecting the licensee to DOS discipline -- including a proceeding for license revocation.
source_note: Real Property Law Section 441-c (license discipline for discriminatory conduct)

topic: Fair Housing, Human Rights Law & Anti-Discrimination
question: If DOS revokes a real estate license based on a finding of unlawful discriminatory conduct under Real Property Law Section 441-c, when may the individual apply to be relicensed?
choice_a: Not until at least one year has passed from the date of revocation
choice_b: The individual may reapply immediately, the same day
choice_c: The individual is permanently barred from ever holding a New York real estate license again, with no exception
choice_d: Relicensing is available after 30 days in every case
explanation: Under Real Property Law Section 441-c, once a real estate broker's or salesperson's license is revoked, the individual is ineligible to be relicensed until at least one year has passed from the date of revocation.
source_note: Real Property Law Section 441-c (relicensing waiting period following revocation)

topic: Fair Housing, Human Rights Law & Anti-Discrimination
question: Federal regulations implementing the Fair Housing Act require most real estate brokerage offices and certain advertisements to display what?
choice_a: The Equal Housing Opportunity poster or logo, informing the public of fair housing rights and the office's commitment to nondiscriminatory practices
choice_b: A copy of the broker's individual license certificate only, with no fair housing content
choice_c: Nothing -- no fair housing display requirement applies to brokerage offices
choice_d: A list of every properly listed property currently for sale in the office
explanation: HUD regulations implementing the Fair Housing Act require conspicuous display of the Equal Housing Opportunity poster or logo in real estate brokerage offices, and its inclusion (or the equivalent slogan) in many forms of real estate advertising, as a visible commitment to fair housing compliance.
source_note: 24 C.F.R. Part 110 (Fair Housing Act implementing regulations -- Equal Housing Opportunity poster/logo requirement)

topic: Fair Housing, Human Rights Law & Anti-Discrimination
question: In an administrative housing discrimination proceeding before a HUD Administrative Law Judge (as opposed to a private lawsuit in federal district court), which remedy is generally NOT available?
choice_a: Punitive damages -- an ALJ may award compensatory damages and impose civil penalties, but punitive damages are generally available only through a private civil action in federal district court
choice_b: Compensatory damages to the victim of discrimination
choice_c: A cease-and-desist order against further discriminatory conduct
choice_d: Any award or penalty whatsoever
explanation: A HUD Administrative Law Judge may award compensatory damages to a discrimination victim and impose civil penalties against the respondent, but generally cannot award punitive damages -- punitive damages are typically available only if the aggrieved party instead pursues (or the case proceeds to) a civil action in federal district court.
source_note: 42 U.S.C. Section 3612 (HUD administrative proceeding remedies) compared with Section 3613 (federal court remedies, including punitive damages)

topic: Fair Housing, Human Rights Law & Anti-Discrimination
question: Under New York's Human Rights Law, the term 'housing accommodation' subject to Section 296(5)'s anti-discrimination provisions extends beyond residential dwellings to also cover what?
choice_a: Land and commercial space, in addition to housing accommodations themselves
choice_b: Only single-family detached homes
choice_c: Only rental apartments, never property offered for sale
choice_d: Nothing beyond residential apartments -- the statute is limited strictly to apartment rentals
explanation: Executive Law Section 296(5)'s protections are not limited to residential apartments -- the statute's coverage extends to housing accommodations, land, and commercial space, reflecting a broader statutory scope than the federal Fair Housing Act's primarily residential focus.
source_note: Executive Law Section 296(5) (NY Human Rights Law -- scope covering housing accommodation, land, and commercial space)
